newsitem.title: USA: Kansas farmers eye feasibility of narrow-row corn.
newsitem.headline: Kansas farmers eye feasibility of narrow-row corn.

text.p: Kansas farmers are looking into boosting corn yields by planting more seeds per acre in narrower rows, agriculture specialists said.

"We don't yet know whether it is feasible in our climate," said Dale Fjell, Kansas State University (KSU) Extension agronomist. "Most of the existing industry and university research on narrow-row corn occurs in the wetter, cloudier climate of the northern Cornbelt."
In 1996, Fjell and fellow KSU agronomists planted narrow-row corn plots on three experimental fields in Kansas, and Fjell said the yield data from the study was "promising."
One of the irrigated fields with a 200-bushel yield average produced an extra 15 bushels per acre. There also was a slight dryland yield increase, Fjell said.

All of the corn plots were treated with recommended herbicides, but weed control was not rated. Still, the researchers observed fewer weeds at harvest in the 15-inch rows seeded at the highest plant populations.

Fjell explained that the greater number of plants per row produced a thicker early leaf canopy to shade out weeds. He also said the greater number of plants could "out-compete" weeds for available soil nutrients.
"Less weed pressure is supposed to be a side benefit of narrow-row corn," he said.

The downside of narrow-row corn is adapting planters and harvesters to fit the rows. Fjell said Kansas growers have tried planting narrow-row corn with a drill in the past, but the seed tended to crack.
"We couldn't get the plant populations low enough without damaging the seed. Drills are designed to handle wheat, soybeans and milo---not corn," Fjell said.
Fjell said he had heard reports of greater yields with plant populations as high as 40,000-plus per acre. But he noted there was a point of diminishing returns.
"Farmers have to weigh the potential for higher yield against the cost of seed. It's pretty expensive to seed a field at 40,000-plus plants per acre," Fjell said.
